tracks.title: Emotional Skills
tracks.description: Twelve weeks of research-informed practice in noticing, naming and regulating emotion, and applying that under criticism, conflict and professional pressure.

lessons.title: What emotions are for
objectives: Describe emotions as signals that prepare action, not as commands.

lessons.title: The emotion chain
objectives: Map an episode as situation, interpretation, body, urge, action, outcome.

lessons.title: Regulation is not suppression
objectives: Contrast suppressing expression with flexible regulation.

lessons.title: How you will learn here
objectives: Use retrieval and spacing to make skills stick.

lessons.title: Emotion granularity
objectives: Use precise emotion words instead of "bad" or "stressed".

lessons.title: Affect labelling
objectives: Name feelings in words to create a small pause.

lessons.title: Mixed and layered emotions
objectives: Recognise that several emotions can co-occur or hide one another.

lessons.title: Body signals
objectives: Locate emotion in the body without judging it.

lessons.title: Urge is not action
objectives: Notice an urge and delay acting on it.

lessons.title: Why venting does not drain anger
Facts versus interpretations
objectives: Separate what happened from what you made it mean.

lessons.title: Generating alternatives
objectives: Produce at least three plausible readings.

lessons.title: Common thinking traps
objectives: Spot mind-reading, catastrophising and all-or-nothing thinking.

lessons.title: Evidence check
objectives: Weigh evidence for and against an interpretation.

lessons.title: Self-distancing
objectives: View an event from a step back.

lessons.title: Temporal distance
objectives: Ask how this will matter in a week, a year.

lessons.title: Acceptance and willingness
objectives: Allow a feeling while acting on what matters.

lessons.title: Problem solving
objectives: Turn a stressor into a next step.

lessons.title: If-then plans
objectives: Pre-commit to responses for predictable triggers.

lessons.title: Rumination versus reflection
objectives: Tell unhelpful loops from useful thinking.

lessons.title: Tolerating uncertainty
objectives: Act well when outcomes are unknown.

lessons.title: Handling setbacks
objectives: Recover from disappointment with a review.

lessons.title: Receiving criticism
objectives: Hear feedback without defending at once.

lessons.title: Sorting feedback
objectives: Separate accurate, partly accurate and inaccurate parts.

lessons.title: Validation
objectives: Acknowledge others' emotions to lower heat.

lessons.title: Decisions under pressure
objectives: Decide well when time is short.

lessons.title: Uncertain outcomes at work
objectives: Stay effective during reorganisations and waiting.

lessons.title: Integration drill
objectives: Use the full chain on a real event.

concepts.label: Given an everyday episode, you can say what the emotion was signalling and show that feeling it did not oblige a particular action.
You can break an episode into situation, interpretation, body, urge, action and outcome, in the right order.
You can tell habitual suppression apart from a deliberate, time-limited choice to hold back, and explain the cost of the habit.
You can explain why retrieval and spacing are used here, and why self-ratings and check scores are kept separate.
Demonstrate the foundations.
You can replace a vague word such as "stressed" with a more precise emotion word that fits the situation.
You can name a feeling in words during an episode and describe what that naming is and is not expected to do.
You can identify two or more emotions present at once, including one that may be hidden by another.
You can run a 30-second check-in: emotion, intensity, and one body signal.
Demonstrate precise noticing and naming.
You can locate and describe bodily signals of an emotion without judging them.
You can notice an urge, name it, and choose whether and when to act on it.
You can explain why venting tends to keep anger going and pick a lower-arousal alternative.
You can carry out a short breathing or grounding reset and say when it fits and when it does not.
Demonstrate body and impulse skills.
You can sort statements about an event into camera facts and interpretations.
You can produce at least three plausible readings of an ambiguous event.
You can spot mind-reading, catastrophising and all-or-nothing thinking without treating every negative thought as a distortion.
You can weigh evidence for and against an interpretation and state what remains uncertain.
Retrieve interpretation skills.
You can describe an event from a self-distanced perspective.
You can use temporal distance to put a current upset in proportion.
You can explain acceptance as allowing a feeling while acting on what matters, not as giving up.
You can produce a fast, fair reappraisal that is not just positive thinking.
Demonstrate interpretation skills (weeks 4-5).
You can name the main strategy families and judge when expressing an emotion fits.
You can match a strategy to emotional intensity.
You can turn a stressor into one concrete next step.
You can write a specific if-then plan for a predictable trigger.
Demonstrate strategy matching.
You can tell rumination from reflection using the "is there a next step?" test.
You can set up and run a worry window.
You can act while uncertain and tell protective avoidance from restrictive avoidance.
You can review a setback for controllable and uncontrollable parts and pick one lesson.
Demonstrate these skills.
You can hear criticism, ask one clarifying question, and delay your evaluation.
You can sort feedback into accurate, partly accurate and inaccurate parts.
You can respond to provocation without escalating, choosing to respond, delay, disengage or set a boundary.
You can plan a difficult conversation: goal, opening line and a fallback.
Retrieve criticism skills.
You can state a boundary assertively, and tell assertive from aggressive and passive responses.
You can make a specific repair after a conflict.
You can validate another person's feeling without having to agree.
You can choose a proportionate response in a conflict scenario and explain its trade-off.
Demonstrate weeks 8-9 skills.
You can stay effective at work while feeling strong emotion, without going cold.
You can answer an excessive demand with options instead of a flat yes or no.
You can use a pressure routine: pause, state the trade-off, decide, set a review point.
You can apply the pressure routine to unfamiliar work scenarios.
Retrieve composure skills.
You can stay effective during workplace uncertainty by separating controllables from rumours.
You can reset after a difficult meeting with a short recovery routine.
You can disagree upward, adapting tactics for unequal power and different incentives.
You can combine composure skills in mixed professional scenarios.
Demonstrate weeks 10-11.
You can describe a recurring pattern without claiming its cause, and explain the role of short-term relief.
You can recognise signs that self-training is not enough and further support is worth seeking.
You can write a realistic maintenance plan.
You can design a small behavioural experiment and revise your hypothesis from the result.
Demonstrate integration.
